bounded_statement: The selected result (two-sample Student t-test over 60 weekly inspection records, t(58) = -41.994, p < 0.001) is not supported as stated: the 60 rows comprise only 12 independent units (module_id), each entered 5 times, so the reported degrees of freedom (58 instead of at most 10 at the module level), t-statistic, and p-value characterization overstate the effective sample size and precision. A module-level reanalysis using the report's own per-module means still yields a -3.000 percentage-point difference with approximately t(10) ≈ -17.9 (p < 0.001), so the direction and approximate magnitude of the effect are robust; only the row-level inferential statistics are invalid.

counterevidence_considered.description: The report's own per-module mean table shows the effect is consistent across every module, and a correct module-level reanalysis (n = 6 vs 6 module means) still gives a -3.000 percentage-point difference with approximately t(10) ≈ -17.9, p < 0.001. The qualitative conclusion therefore does not depend on the pseudoreplicated procedure; only the reported test statistics do.
counterevidence_considered.observed_value: module-level means: nanocoat 1.6-2.3%, bare 4.5-5.4%; module-level t ≈ -17.9 on 10 df

counterevidence_considered.description: The report transparently discloses its assumption that each inspection record is an independent observation and accurately describes the design (12 modules, 5 weekly inspections), so the flaw is an incorrect analysis choice openly stated rather than a concealed manipulation; this does not, however, make the stated t(58) inference valid.

extensions.x-stage1-falsification-attempt: I attempted to falsify the issue three ways. (1) I checked whether the workflow aggregates to one value per module before testing: losses() appends one value per CSV row and build_report() passes the resulting 30-element lists directly to stats.ttest_ind, with dof = 60 - 2 = 58, confirming row-level entry with no aggregation, clustering, or mixed-effects handling anywhere in analysis.py. (2) I checked whether rows sharing a module_id could plausibly be independent units: data-description.md explicitly states the same twelve modules were revisited weekly and names module_id as the independent-unit column, ruling this out. (3) I tested whether the flaw is materially consequential by recomputing the test at the module level from the report's per-module means (nanocoat: 1.6, 1.8, 2.0, 2.1, 2.3, 2.2; bare: 4.5, 4.8, 5.1, 5.0, 5.4, 5.2): the difference remains -3.000 points with pooled-variance t ≈ -17.9 on 10 df. The direction survives, but the reported t(58) = -41.994 and its implied precision do not match any valid unit-level analysis, so the falsification attempts failed to overturn the finding that the stated statistical result rests on repeated entry of independent units into a row-independent procedure.

root_cause: The workflow's losses() function returns one power_loss_pct value per CSV row and build_report() passes the pooled 30-vs-30 row-level lists directly to scipy.stats.ttest_ind with dof = len(treated) + len(control) - 2 = 58. No per-module aggregation or dependence-aware model is applied, so the five repeated weekly readings from each of the 12 independent modules (independent-unit column module_id, per data-description.md) are each entered as separate independent observations into a procedure that assumes row independence.
